summary:
Mexico has no national administrative procedure for legal gender recognition; the process is set state by state, so a trans visitor's document status depends on which of the country's 32 states they are in. As of March 2025, 22 states had legislated an administrative recognition procedure, two more operated one in practice without legislative enactment, and six state legislatures had enacted nothing at all.

Only seven states extend recognition to children and adolescents. In 2022 the Supreme Court of Mexico set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to minors, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where no procedure exists, trans people are left carrying identity documents that contradict their lived gender, and that mismatch drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

Tabasco has no legal gender-recognition procedure, Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion reported on 6 March 2024. Without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or close appearance scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans residents are shut out of employment, health services, education and financial transactions.

Lethal violence is persistent. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, and the killings drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100 for the same period.

Trans women were killed in the same period in circumstances that recur in the record: Karina Gómez was murdered in Villahermosa in August 2023, and a trans woman was found dead in the Carrizal River that month.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety.
tangentialFactors:
Impunity is the backdrop against which any legal protection operates. More than 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice. The analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction. That stability contrasts with the recognition regime for gender, which Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 remains uneven, calling on the states without administrative procedures to adopt them.

Regional comparison places Mexico among the worst-affected countries. Transgender Europe's 52 recorded transfeminicidios between October 2022 and September 2023 were exceeded only by Brazil's 100 in the same twelve months.
localsOnly:
Recognition is pursued through the state a resident lives in, not through a national office, and the outcome differs sharply across the federation: 22 states have legislated procedures, two operate one without legislative enactment, and six have nothing on the books. Residents of those six states have no local route to correcting their documents.

Only seven states extend recognition to children and adolescents, so families seeking documents for a trans minor depend on where they are registered. The Supreme Court's 2022 guidelines bind the states and extended the right to minors, but Human Rights Watch found in March 2025 that implementation still differs from state to state.

Tabasco illustrates the daily cost. Human Rights Watch and the Community Center for Inclusion reported on 6 March 2024 that trans residents there live without documents that match their gender, are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions, and face violence, harassment and humiliation whenever they present identification. The murder of Karina Gómez in Villahermosa in August 2023 sits within that same context.

Same-sex marriage has been available since 2009, so partnership recognition does not present the obstacle that gender documentation does for residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
The six state legislatures that had enacted no recognition procedure as of March 2025 are not identified in the sources assembled here; only Guanajuato and Tabasco are named in connection with documented incidents.

No sourced material in this inventory addresses border formalities, visa screening or inspection of gender markers on passports at the point of entry, so visitor-side entry practice remains unresolved.

Whether the state-level figures have shifted after March 2025, and whether the two states operating a procedure without legislative enactment have since enacted one, are not sourced here.

The enforcement record of the Paola Buenrostro law since it was approved in July 2024, including any prosecutions for transfemicide under it, is not documented in this inventory.
